==Trademark strategy==

The V850 is an [[unregistered trademark]] but not a [[trademark|registered one]].<ref name="TM-Notice">
{{cite web|title=Trademark Notice|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/legal/trademarks.html|website=www.renesas.com|publisher=Renesas}}
</ref>
NEC once applied for a trademark to be registered with the [[Japan Patent Office]], but it was rejected,<ref>
{{cite web|title=Trademark application T2001-067573|url=https://www.j-platpat.inpit.go.jp/web/TR/JP4_2001067573/52BA76A66EBA5C36B1F0A6753F275D8F|date=2001-07-25|quote=Result: application refused}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=V850 Embedded Microcontroller|url=https://www.tmdn.org/tmview/get-detail?st13=JP502001000067573|website=www.tmdn.org|language=en|date=2004-12-18|quote=Result: application refused}}
</ref>
as it was a natural extension of the series number.
However, this action has been enough to prevent other people or organizations from registering it as a trademark. In addition, Renesas has been using the V850X/xxn type trademark, such as V850E/MA1, for more than 20 years, because the combination of one alphabetical with two numerical characters cannot be granted as a registered trademark. It is thus free to use without registration.

One exception is V850E/PHO3 (PHOENIX 3, or PHOENIX-FS).<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Schmerling|first1=Holger|title=AUTOSAR FlexRay driver now available for microcontrollers|journal=System@IC News|date=2006|volume=2006|issue=4|page=3|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/c4cb/c862d757e6f7575f6e82653171bc035e525f.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180302103956/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/c4cb/c862d757e6f7575f6e82653171bc035e525f.pdf|archive-date=2018-03-02|publisher=NEC Electronics|s2cid=15509410|language=en}}
</ref>{{rp|3}}<ref>
{{cite book|title=V850E/PH2: Hardware|date=January 2007|publisher=NEC Electronics|url=http://pdf.datasheet.live/datasheets-1/renesas_electronics/UPD70F3187GD_A1_-64-LML.pdf|page=33|edition=1.00|ref=U16580EE3V1UD00}}
</ref>{{rp|33}}
Another usage of PHOENIX 3 by Renesas Electronics is the COOL PHOENIX 3, which employs the ARM Cortex-M0 core.<ref>
{{cite book|title=Quick time-to-market with Renesas Synergy Platform and Cool Phoenix 3|date=October 2016|publisher=Renesas|edition=1.00|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-eu/doc/DocumentServer/012/R30PF0110ED0100.pdf|ref=R30PF0110ED0100|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180302163938/https://www.renesas.com/en-eu/doc/DocumentServer/012/R30PF0110ED0100.pdf|archive-date=2018-03-02|url-status=dead}}
</ref>
PHOENIX 3 is a registered trademark of [[the 3DO Company]] as [[USPTO]] Reg. 2,009,119.<ref>
{{cite web|title=TMVIEW: PHOENIX 3|url=https://www.tmdn.org/tmview/get-detail?st13=US500000074656346|website=www.tmdn.org}}
</ref>

According to current Renesas Electronics documentation, at least the following strings are regarded as its trademark: "V800 Series", "V850 family", "V850/SA1", "V850/SB1", "V850/SB2", "V850/SF1", "V850/SV1", "V850E/MA1", "V850E/MA2", "V850E/IA1", "V850E/IA2", "V850E/MS1", "V850E/MS2", "V851", "V852", "V853", "V854", "V850", "V850E", and "V850ES".<ref name="TM-Notice"/><ref name="V850-Arch"/>

Because the V850 trademark has been used for more than 20 years, most people do not know that the RH850 family is based on an extension of the V850 instruction set architecture, and has backward compatibility with V850, V850E, V850ES, and V850E2. The RH850 is consequently thought of as being without the legacy software compatibility of the V850.<ref>
{{cite web|title=RH何某というのはSHのコアなのですか？|url=https://japan.renesasrulz.com/cafe_rene/f/forum15/4070/rh-sh?pi4368=1|website=Renesas Rulz - Japan|publisher=Renesas Electronics|language=ja|date=2017-03-29|trans-title=Does RH-something employ SH core?|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180205072642/https://japan.renesasrulz.com/cafe_rene/f/forum15/4070/rh-sh?pi4368=1|archive-date=2018-02-05|url-status=deviated}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=Could anyone please tells me the major differences between the RH850 and V850 families ? {{!}} GNU Tools|url=https://gcc-renesas.com/question/tells-major-differences-rh850-v850-families/|website=gcc-renesas.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180205184425/https://gcc-renesas.com/question/tells-major-differences-rh850-v850-families/|archive-date=2018-02-05|url-status=dead}}
</ref>

==Development methodology==

[[File:V810_01.jpg|thumb|V810 mounted on [[:ja:PC-FXGA|''PC-FXGA'' (in Japanese)]]<ref>
{{cite web|title=PC-FXGA – WIP|url=https://cdromrom.wordpress.com/pc-fxga-wip/|website=Super CD·Rom<sup>2</sup> à GoGo|date=2015-12-13}}
</ref>
''Gaming Accelerator'' board.<br/>Marked as "©NEC 1991." ]]
[[File:Nintendo-Virtual-Boy-Motherboard-Flat.jpg|thumb |[[Nintendo]] ''[[Virtual Boy]]'' employed customized V810. 14x20mm<sup>2</sup> packge (on left) is marked "©NEC '91, '93."]]

Because the V850&nbsp;family<ref name="V850-Arch">
{{cite book|title=V850 FAMILY 32-bit Single-Chip Microcontroller Architecture|date=March 2001|publisher=Renesas Electronics|edition=7th|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/020/U10243EJ7V0UM00.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127202636/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/020/U10243EJ7V0UM00.pdf|archive-date=2018-01-27|url-status=dead}}
</ref>{{rp|16}}
was developed as a branch of the V800&nbsp;series,<ref name="cat99"/>{{rp|97, PDF103}}
the basic CPU architecture is inherited from the V810.<ref name="V810-Arch">{{cite book|title=V810 FAMILY 32-bit Microprocessor Architecture|date=October 1995|publisher=NEC Corporation|edition=1st|url=http://www.planetvb.com/content/downloads/documents/U10082EJ1V0UM00.pdf|access-date=2018-02-02|archive-date=2016-12-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161223133902/http://www.planetvb.com/content/downloads/documents/U10082EJ1V0UM00.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The instruction set architecture of the first V850 is drastically modified from that of the V810, but the difference is within a patch level from the GNU Compiler Collection point of view.<ref name="Newer-gccVB"/> The main purpose of this change is to implement [[saturation arithmetic]] at customers' request.
[[File:NEC UPD705103 v833 MCU.jpg|thumb|A v833 CPU, a pin-compatible revision of the v832 CPU.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Pioneer |url=http://archive.org/details/avicd3xuuc |title=Pioneer Car Stereo System AVIC-D3 Service Manual |date=2007-02-01 |page=262}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Renesas |url=https://www.renesas.com/us/en/document/mah/v832tm-hardware-preliminary |title=V832 32-bit Microprocessor Hardware uPD705102 Preliminary User's Manual |date=1999-04-01 |page=27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2004-03-01 |title=PRODUCT STATUS & PHASE-OUT LIST MARCH 2004 |url=http://www.ee.nec.de:80/_Upd/Prod_Status.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040413031732/http://www.ee.nec.de:80/_Upd/Prod_Status.pdf |archive-date=2004-04-13 |website=NEC Electronics (Europe) GmbH |page=11}}</ref> This microprocessor was used in car navigation systems during the 2000s, mostly made by [[Pioneer Corporation]] and [[Alpine Electronics]].]]
The detailed design methodology of the V810 is described in this journal.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Suzuki|first1=Hiroaki|last2=Suzuki|first2=Chika|last3=Kimura|first3=Akiko|last4=Sato|first4=Syoichiro|last5=Ide|first5=Syuichi|last6=Sakanaka|first6=Yasuhide|title=A 32 - Bit RISC Microprocessor V810 and its design techniques.|journal=SIG SLDM Technical Reports|date=1993-01-22|volume=1993|issue=6|pages=155–162|url=https://ipsj.ixsq.nii.ac.jp/ej/?action=repository_uri&item_id=28087&file_id=1&file_no=1|series=1992-SLDM-065|publisher=Information Processing Society of Japan|language=ja|format=PDF|id=AA11451459|quote=<br/>Abstract:<br/>An advanced 32-bit RISC microprocessor for embedded controls; V810 and its design technique are described in this paper. The V810 is fabricated by using 0.8μm CMOS double metal layer process technology to integrate 240,000 transistors on a 7.7×7.7mm<sup>2</sup> die. In design of the V810, we used design automation techniques. The V810 was analyzed for logical correctness and timing constraint before fabrication. Finally, V810 executed realtime-OS and SPEC benchmarks correctly at first silicons.}}
</ref>
The V850 utilizes these design assets; but the [[datapath]] logic was changed from [[Dynamic logic (digital electronics)|dynamic logic]] to [[static logic]], to enable 32.768&nbsp;kHz [[real-time clock]] frequency operation mode.

The [[register-transfer level]] "CPU architecture design" of the V810 is developed with the Functional Description Language (FDL)<ref>
{{cite journal |last1=Akaboshi |first1=Hiroki |last2=Yasuura |first2=Hiroto |title=Design Comparison of Hardware Description Languages in RT Level |url=https://ipsj.ixsq.nii.ac.jp/ej/?action=repository_uri&item_id=27938&file_id=1&file_no=1 |date=8 March 1995 |journal=IPSJ SIG Notes |volume=1995 |issue=24 (1994-SLDM-074) |pages=57–64  |publisher=Information Processing Society of Japan |language=ja |format=PDF |access-date=23 September 2022 |quote=<br />Abstract:<br />Progress of logic/layout synthesis makes it possible to design circuits by Hardware Description Languages (HDLs). When a designed circuit is small, it is synthesized automatically from HDL description. In this paper, to make it clear what kinds of problems are there in designing a large circuit looks like a processor, we design a processor and some components of it by HDLs in RT level and evaluate circuits synthesized by a logic/layout synthesis tool.}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite book |doi=10.1145/74382.74414|chapter-url=https://www.cs.york.ac.uk/rts/docs/DAC-1964-2005/PAPERS/1989/DAC89_185.PDF |isbn=0-89791-310-8|chapter=Locating functional errors in logic circuits |title=Proceedings of the 1989 26th ACM/IEEE conference on Design automation conference - DAC '89 |pages=185–191 |year=1989 |last1=Tamura |first1=K. A. |s2cid=2364060 }}
</ref><ref>
{{cite conference |last1=Kato|first1=S.|last2=Sasaki|first2=T.|title=FDL: A Structural Behavior Description Language |book-title=Computer Hardware Description Languages and Their Applications: Proceedings of the IFIP WG 10.2 Sixth International Symposium on Computer Hardware Description Languages and Their Applications |date=1983|pages=137–152|isbn=978-0-444-86633-2|publisher=Elsevier Science}}
</ref>
on the Falcon Simulator software, which are NEC's [[wikt:Special:Search/in house#English|in-house]] [[CAD]] tools.
This methodology is the same as that used for the [[NEC V60]].<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Yano|first1=Yoichi|title=32ビット・マイコン「V60」開発物語|journal=Encor|date=April 2012|issue=75|pages=17–20|url=http://www.shmj.or.jp/dev_story/pdf/develop46.pdf|trans-title=Development story of the V60; a 32-bit microprocessor|publisher=Society of Semiconductor Industry Specialists|language=ja}}
</ref>
In the late 1980s, the [[Verilog HDL]] had not yet been acquired by [[Cadence Design Systems]].<ref>
{{cite book|last1=Sutherland|first1=Stuart|title=The Verilog PLI Handbook: A User's Guide and Comprehensive Reference on the Verilog Programming Language Interface|date=2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4615-5017-4|page=3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LGTSBwAAQBAJ&q=Verilog+Cadence+1990&pg=PA3|language=en}}
</ref>
FDL had been used until the middle of the 2000s, and was also used for the development of NEC's [[super-computer]] named [[Earth Simulator]].<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Inasaka|first1=Jun|last2=Ikeda|first2=Rikikazu|last3=Umezawa|first3=Kazuhiko|last4=Yoshikawa|first4=Ko|last5=Yamada|first5=Shitaka|last6=Kitawaki|first6=Shigemune|title=Hardware Technology of the Earth Simulator|journal=NEC Research and Development|date=January 2003|volume=44|issue=1|pages=27–36|url=https://www.jamstec.go.jp/es-repository/metadb/up/191/rd07.pdf|series=Architecture and Hardware for HPC}}
</ref>

The difference from V60 is that the [[circuit diagram]] was written with a [[schematic editor]], not of [[Calma]] but of [[Mentor Graphics]], called NETED,<ref>
{{cite web|title=Trademarks|url=https://www.mentor.com/terms_conditions/trademarks|website=www.mentor.com|publisher=Mentor Graphics|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180204123921/https://www.mentor.com/terms_conditions/trademarks|archive-date=2018-02-04|url-status=deviated}}
</ref>
a part of the Design Architect product<ref>
{{cite web|title=Mentor Graphics and Pyxis Technology|url=https://www.mentor.com/products/ic_nanometer_design/pyxis|website=www.mentor.com|publisher=Mentor Graphics|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809110643/https://www.mentor.com/products/ic_nanometer_design/pyxis|archive-date=2019-08-09|url-status=deviated}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=IC Nanometer Design Tutorials – Santa Clara University|url=https://www.mentor.com/company/higher_ed/services_support/ic_tutorial|website=www.mentor.com|publisher=Santa Clara University|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180204182254/https://www.mentor.com/company/higher_ed/services_support/ic_tutorial|archive-date=2018-02-04|url-status=deviated}}
</ref>
on [[Apollo Computer]]'s [[workstation]], which was the major schematic editor at that moment.<ref>
{{cite book|last1=Jansen|first1=Dirk|title=The Electronic Design Automation Handbook|date=2010-02-23|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-0-387-73543-6|page=54|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=br3gBwAAQBAJ&q=%22NETED%22+Mentor%20Graphics&pg=PA54|language=en|quote=<br/>Design Architect by Mentor Graphics Corporation with programs NETED and SYMED. This system is the most universal one of the three [3.3].<br/>Version C1 on HP Unix V10.20 is used (short form MENTOR)}}
</ref>
It enabled designers to generate [[netlist]]s, such as [[EDIF]] and [[SPICE]], for [[Layout Versus Schematic|LVS]] programs like Cadence's [[ECAD, Inc.|Dracula]] products, and NEC's in-house Zycad netlist for [[logic simulation]]. Later on, this circuit diagram of NETED was able to generate a [[Digital circuit|gate-level]] Verilog HDL netlist for V850.

Most of the register-transfer-level FDL netlist was translated to the gate-level [[schematic]] by hand, because the [[logic synthesis]] had not yet to be practical.
The FDL was precisely divided into datapath and random logic. For the datapath part,
the gate-level circuit diagram enabled manually repeated [[Integrated circuit layout|artwork]]. On the other hand, for the random logic part, logic synthesis was tried for generating gate-level schematic, but it was only about 10% of the total circuit.

In addition, [[formal verification]] was also not yet practical, which meant that full [[regression test]] by [[dynamic simulation|dynamic]] logic simulation was required for the gate-level netlist to compare with the RTL one. For gate-level logic simulation, NEC's in-house CAD tool V-SIM was usually used.<ref>
{{cite report |title=CB-C8 3-VOLT, 0.5-MICRON CELL-BASED CMOS ASIC |url=http://www.piclist.com/techref/nec/cbc8hd.pdf |date=July 1994 |page=7 |publisher=NEC |language=en |access-date=23 September 2022}}
</ref>
But sometimes a [[hardware emulator]], such as Zycad LE simulation accelerator,<ref>
{{cite book|last1=Harlow III|first1=Justin E.|title=What Every Engineer Should Know about Engineering Workstations|date=1986|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-0-8247-7509-4|page=47|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zC_lDTNdu8MC&q=Zycad-LE&pg=PA47|language=en}}
</ref>
was used for this purpose.
(Refer to:.<ref>
{{cite web|last1=Kang|first1=Sungho|title=Verification I|publisher=Yonsei University.|url=http://soc.yonsei.ac.kr/class/material/CAD/Verification1-Hardware%20Accelation.pdf}}
</ref>{{rp|13}}
In this material, the performance of Zycad LE is compared with NEC's HAL, but initial design decade differs.<ref>
{{cite book |doi= 10.1109/DAC.1986.1586146|chapter-url=https://www.cs.york.ac.uk/rts/docs/DAC-1964-2005/PAPERS/1986/DAC86_581.PDF |isbn=0-8186-0702-5|chapter=HAL II: A Mixed Level Hardware Logic Simulation System |title=23rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference |pages=581–587 |year=1986 |last1=Takasaki |first1=S. |last2=Sasaki |first2=T. |last3=Nomizu |first3=N. |last4=Ishikura |first4=H. |last5=Koike |first5=N. }}
</ref>)

==Architecture==

===Basic architecture===

The basis of the V810 and V850 has a typical [[general-purpose register]]s-based [[load/store architecture]].<ref name="V810-seminar">{{cite web|title=V810 Seminar|url=http://www.planetvb.com/content/downloads/documents/V810%20Seminar.pdf|publisher=NEC Corporation|language=en|date=1995-02-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414124958/http://www.planetvb.com/content/downloads/documents/V810%20Seminar.pdf|archive-date=2016-04-14|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{rp|4}}
There are 32 32-bit general-purpose registers. Register 0 (R0) is fixed as the Zero Register which always contains zero.
In the V850, R30 is implicitly used by the <code>sld</code> and <code>sst</code> instructions. 16-bit short-format load/store instructions use [[Pointer (computer programming)|element pointer (ep)]], where the [[addressing mode]] comprises the base address register ep and immediate-operand offsets.
In V850E or later [[microarchitecture]]s, R3 is implicitly used by <code>PREPARE/DISPOSE</code>; [[call stack]] frame creation; and unwinding instructions, as a [[stack pointer]]. Compilers' [[calling convention]]s also use R3 as the stack pointer.

The original V850 has a simple 5-stage 1-clock pitch [[Instruction pipelining|pipeline]] architecture.<ref name="V810-seminar"/{{rp|6}}<ref name="V850-Arch"/>{{rp|114–126}}
This is a significant feature of [[reduced instruction set computer]]s (RISCs). But the object-code size is about half that of the [[MIPS architecture processors|MIPS]] [[R3000]],<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|5}} because the V810 and V850 adopted 16-bit and 32-bit 2-way form-length instruction formats, respectively,<ref name="V850-Arch"/>{{rp|38–40}}<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|17}}<ref name="V810-Arch" />{{rp|29–30}}
and most of the frequently used instructions are mapped onto a 16-bit half-word. In other words, a 16-bit external bus width is enough to provide instructions continuously without pipeline stalling, which enables low power consumption on the application board, and is suitable for mobile equipment. This concept is similar to [[SuperH|Renesas (formerly, Hitachi) SH]], [[ARM architecture#Thumb|ARM Thumb]], and [[MIPS architecture#MIPS16|MIPS16]] instruction set architectures.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Engblom|first1=Jakob|title=Embedded Systems Computer Architecture|journal=Extended Abstract from ESSES 2003|date=2003|s2cid=15760973|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/a7ae/f8e8d1680a29e631a8b10072bd63d5c52559.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180225064824/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/a7ae/f8e8d1680a29e631a8b10072bd63d5c52559.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-25|quote=<br/>Code size is an important factor in most embedded designs, and instruction sets are designed and extended with code size in mind. Fairly typically, the NEC V850 architecture uses 16-, 32-, 48-bit, and 64-bit instructions to encode a RISC-style instruction set. The 32-bit ARM and MIPS architecture have been extended with reduced 16-bit instruction sets in order to reduce the code size. Instructions that perform a lot of work, like loading multiple values from the stack, are popular to reduce code size.}}
</ref>{{rp|4}}

In addition, the [[instruction set]] is carefully implemented. For example, to execute a [[function call]] with a Jump and (Register) Link instruction,<ref name="V850-Arch"/>{{rp|61}}<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|20}}<ref name="V810-Arch"/>{{rp|64}} which saves the next [[program counter]] (PC) on a register (fixed to R31 in V810), is also one of the RISC techniques to reduce the number of instructions. Return from the [[Subroutine|function]] can be accomplished by <code>jmp [Rn]</code> (<code>jmp [R31]</code> in V810) instruction.<ref name="V850-Arch"/>{{rp|61}}<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|23}}<ref name="V810-Arch"/>{{rp|65}} Typical [[CISC processor]]s use call and return instructions and push the next PC on their [[stack memory]] area.

But V810 and V850 have some microarchitecture differences. The V810 adopts a [[Control unit#Microprogram control unit|microprogram operation]] method for some instructions, such as [[floating-point arithmetic]] and [[bit string]] operations, while the V850 uses a one-hundred-percent [[Control unit#Hardwired control unit|hardwired control]] method. As a result, for example, the first V850 does not have floating-point arithmetic and [[Bit Manipulation Instruction Sets|bit manipulation instruction sets]], including the [[Find first set|"find first one/zero" (search 1/0; <code>SCH1x</code>/<code>SCH0x</code>)]], except for "set/clr/negate a bit" (<code>SET1</code>/<code>CLR1</code>/<code>NOT1</code>). Those extended instruction sets are revived in V850E2x extensions.

Though the V800 series adopts a RISC instruction set architecture, their [[assembly language]] is [[hand-coding]] friendly. They adopt a straightforward load/store architecture.<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|4}} In addition, the "[[Interlock (engineering)#Microprocessors|interlock]]" mechanism, both for the [[Classic RISC pipeline#Data hazards|data hazards]] and for the [[Hazard (computer architecture)#Control hazards (branch hazards)|branch hazards]], are implemented:<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|33–35}} in other words, an assembly language programmer does not need to consider any [[delay slot]]s. 32 general-purpose registers provide flexibility for assembly language users. A mixture of hand-assembled codes and [[C language]] compiled codes is facilitated by using compiler options, such as "<code>-mno-app-regs</code>" in the [[Gnu Compiler Collection]].<ref>{{cite web|title=GCC: V850 Options|url=https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-7.3.0/gcc/V850-Options.html#V850-Options|website=gcc.gnu.org|publisher=Free Software Foundation, Inc.}}</ref>

The <code>IN</code> instruction of the V810, which enables unsigned-load from [[memory-mapped I/O]], was removed from the first V850s.<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|22}}<ref name="V810-Arch"/>{{rp|63}}

Detailed discussions are available in some old journals.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Kaneko|first1=Hiroaki|last2=Sakurai|first2=Yoshikazu|last3=Nasu|first3=Masaki|last4=Katsuta|first4=Hiroshi|last5=Nagasaki|first5=Kazunori|last6=Hiiragizawa|first6=Yasunori|last7=Sonobe|first7=Satoru|last8=Onishi|first8=Tatsuro|last9=Tokunaga|first9=Kei|title=高性能・低消費電力動作の32ビットRISCシングルチップマイクロコンピュータV851|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=March 1995|volume=48|issue=3|pages=42–48|url=http://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/detail?JGLOBAL_ID=200902102316525767&q=High%20Performance%20and%20Low-Power-Consumption%2032-bit%20RISC%20Single%20Chip%20Microcomputer%20V851.&t=0|series=Special Issue on Semiconductor Devices.|trans-title=High Performance and Low-Power-Consumption 32-bit RISC Single Chip Microcomputer V851.|publisher=NEC Corporation|language=ja|issn=0285-4139}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Yamagata|first1=Yasushi|last2=Ishibashi|first2=Takashi|last3=Sano|first3=Yuichi|last4=Koga|first4=Yoshikazu|last5=Yoshida|first5=Miho|last6=Sugo|first6=Akihisa|title=32ビットRISCマイクロコントローラV853|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=April 1996|volume=49|issue=3|pages=55–60|url=http://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/detail?JGLOBAL_ID=200902197739625440|series=Special Issue: Semiconductor Devices.|trans-title=32-bit RISC Microcontroller V853.|publisher=NEC Corporation|language=ja|issn=0285-4139}}
</ref>

===Instruction set extensions===

The V850 series added many instruction set extensions, but all the extensions have [[backward compatibility]].<ref name="EET-SIMD">
{{cite magazine|last1=Krämer|first1=Michael|title=Latest 32-bit RISC architecture for automotive expands functionality|url=https://www.eetimes.com/latest-32-bit-risc-architecture-for-automotive-expands-functionality/|magazine=EE Times|language=en|date=2011-01-21|quote=<br/>All V850 products are upwards compatible. As a result, today's sophisticated components can still execute the same instructions as their forebears. The architecture has undergone continual improvements with extensions to the instruction set, and today it offers computing power of up to 2.6 Dhrystone MIPS/MHz. Further performance increases can be achieved by integrating several of these processor cores on a single chip, delivering twice or even four times more computing power.}}
</ref>
Therefore, older software designed for the previous versions of the V850 work on new V850 cores.

The first generation of the V850 does not have [[unsigned (arithmetic)|unsigned]] load instructions, which had been removed from the V810 (where it was implemented with <code>IN.H</code> and <code>IN.B</code>). Then, in the second generation V850E (V850E1) Series, such unsigned functionality was again added (with <code>LD.HU</code> and <code>LD.BU</code>). In addition, the V850E has some other user-friendly "[[Complex instruction set computing|CISCy]]" extensions, such as <code>call table</code>, <code>switch</code>,  and <code>prepare/dispose</code>.<ref>
{{cite book|title=V850E1 for Architecture|date=2004-02-01|publisher=Renesas|edition=3.01|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/022/U14559EJ3V1UM00.pdf|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127202714/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/022/U14559EJ3V1UM00.pdf|archive-date=2018-01-27|url-status=dead}}
</ref>{{rp|217}}

In 1996, the V853 was announced as the first 32-bit RISC [[microcontroller]] with integrated [[flash memory]]<ref name="BizWire-V853">{{cite press release |title=First 32-bit RISC Microcontroller with Integrated Flash Memory Offered by NEC Electronics Newest Product in Company's V800 Series Operates at 33 MHz. |url=https://www.thefreelibrary.com/First+32-bit+RISC+Microcontroller+with+Integrated+Flash+Memory...-a018052638 |website=www.thefreelibrary.com |publisher=BUSINESS WIRE |date=1996-03-04 |access-date=2018-02-26 |archive-date=2018-02-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226152021/https://www.thefreelibrary.com/First+32-bit+RISC+Microcontroller+with+Integrated+Flash+Memory...-a018052638 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
but its maximum number of "erase and write" cycles was 16.<ref>
{{cite book|title=UPD70F3003A,70F3025A,70F3003A(A) Data Sheet|date=2005-08-01|publisher=Renesas|page=37|edition=5.01|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/021/U13189EJ5V1DS00.pdf|ref=U13189EJ5V1DS00|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226211704/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/021/U13189EJ5V1DS00.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-26|url-status=dead}}
</ref>{{rp|37}}

In 1998, NEC strategically started to expand the V850 product line, to standard [[Application-specific integrated circuit#Application-specific standard product|application-specific standard product]] (ASSP), [[application-specific integrated circuit]] (ASIC), and [[system on a chip]] (SoC) businesses.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Matsumoto|first1=Yoichi|title=NEXT STEP: NEC'S STRATEGY FOR RISC MICROCOMPUTERS|journal=NEC Device Technology International|date=1999|volume=1999|issue=5|url=https://www.usbid.com/datasheets/usbid/2000/2000-q2/dti55nsz.pdf|publisher=NEC|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180209002740/https://www.usbid.com/datasheets/usbid/2000/2000-q2/dti55nsz.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-09|url-status=dead}}
</ref>

In 2001, NEC launched the V850ES core, which is an ultra-low-power series, but is ISA-compatible with the V850E.<ref name="NEC: Press Release">{{cite press release|title=NEC Launches 32-Bit RISC Single-chip Microcontroller for Ultra-low-power Mobile Applications|url=http://www.nec.co.jp/press/en/0108/2301.html|website=www.nec.co.jp|publisher=NEC: Press Release|language=en|date=2001-08-23}}</ref>

Around 2001, the Java Acceleration IP core for the V850 seemed to be provided to some customers in SoCs<ref>
{{cite press release|title=NEC Releases Java Accelerator for 32-Bit RISC V850 Microcontrollers|url=http://www.nec.co.jp/press/en/0111/1501.html|website=www.nec.co.jp|publisher=NEC|language=en|date=2001-11-15}}
</ref>
but detailed information is only found in some patents.<ref>
{{cite web|last1=Aoki|first1=Yayoi|title=US 6,948,034 B2; Method for use of stack|url=http://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/.piw?PageNum=0&docid=06948034|website=pdfpiw.uspto.gov|format=PDF|date=2001-11-30|quote=The present invention relates to a method for use of a stack in a Java accelerator device.}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|last1=Mine|first1=Kazumasa|title=US 7,200,741 B1: Microprocessor having main processor and co-processor|url=http://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/.piw?PageNum=0&docid=07200741|website=pdfpiw.uspto.gov|publisher=United States Patent and Trademark Office|language=en|format=PDF|date=2000-11-21|quote=With such arrangement, the microprocessor can flexibly deal with various kinds of instruction sets with different architectures such as an instruction set for an interpreter language for realizing a virtual machine for Java and an instruction set for emulating another microprocessor.}}
</ref>

In 2005, NEC Electronics introduced the V850E2 core as the V850E2/ME3 product line with [[super-scalar architecture]].<ref>{{cite press release |title=NEC Electronics Introduces 32-Bit V850E2/ME3 Microcontroller for High-Performance, Real-Time Processing; Most Advanced V850 Microcontroller Enables Performance of 400MIPS at 200MHz. |url=https://www.thefreelibrary.com/NEC+Electronics+Introduces+32-Bit+V850E2%2fME3+Microcontroller+for...-a0128614670 |website=www.thefreelibrary.com |date=2005 |access-date=2018-02-26|archive-date=2018-02-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226152019/https://www.thefreelibrary.com/NEC+Electronics+Introduces+32-Bit+V850E2%2fME3+Microcontroller+for...-a0128614670 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2009, NEC Electronics introduced the V850E2M as dual-core with 2.56MIPS/MHz and 1.5 mW/MIPS.<ref name="Biz-wire-2009">
{{cite web|title=NEC Electronics Introduces Next-Generation V850E2M Dual-Core Architecture For 32-Bit V850 Microcontrollers|url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20090420006518/en/NEC-Electronics-Introduces-Next-Generation-V850E2M-Dual-Core-Architecture|website=www.businesswire.com|publisher=Business Wire|language=en|date=2009-04-20}}
</ref>

In 2011, Renesas first introduced the [[SIMD]] extension for the V850 into the V850E2H core.<ref name="EET-SIMD"/><ref>
{{cite web|last1=Whytock|first1=Paul|title=Next-Gen 32Bit V850 CPU Core Features SIMD Support|url=http://www.electronicdesign.com/dsps/next-gen-32bit-v850-cpu-core-features-simd-support|website=Electronic Design|date=2010-10-14}}
</ref>
As for the SIMD extension, some academic studies were done on instruction encoding and efficient SIMD code generation.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Kumura|first1=Takahiro|last2=Taga|first2=Soichiro|last3=Ishiura|first3=Nagisa|last4=Takeuchi|first4=Yoshinori|last5=Imai|first5=Masaharu|title=Software Development Tool Generation Method Suitable for Instruction Set Extension of Embedded Processors|journal=IPSJ Transactions on System LSI Design Methodology|date=2025-04-13|volume=3|pages=207–221 |doi=10.2197/ipsjtsldm.3.207|language=en|issn=1882-6687|doi-access=free}}
</ref> It was later added into the V850G3H, V850G3KH and other H-extension cores before Renesas changed the V850 name to "RH850". Unfortunately, there is almost no publicly available documentation for these cores because Renesas gated them under [[non-disclosure agreements]] (NDAs) that were only signed by automotive manufacturers.

===Power consumption===

The original V810 and V850 CPU architecture is designed for [[ultra-low power]] applications.

The V810 is described in detail in some journals.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Harigai|first1=Hisao|last2=Kusuda|first2=Masahiro|last3=Kojima|first3=Shingo|last4=Moriyama|first4=Masatoshi|last5=Ienaga|first5=Takashi|last6=Yano|first6=Yoichi|title=A low power consumption and low voltage operation 32-bit RISC Microprocessor|journal=SIG ARC Technical Reports|date=1992-10-22|volume=1992|issue=82 (1992-ARC-096)|pages=41–48|url=https://ipsj.ixsq.nii.ac.jp/ej/?action=repository_uri&item_id=24393&file_id=1&file_no=1|publisher=Information Processing Society of Japan|language=ja|format=PDF|id=AN10096105|quote=<br/>Abstract:<br/>An advanced 32-bit RISC microprocessor for embedded control; V810 is introduced in this paper. The V810 has high performance and application specified functions.<br/>V810 dissipates less power than any other RISC chips. The V810 is the first 32-bit RISC microprocessor that operates at 2.2 V.<br/>The V810 chip is fabricated by using 0.8 μm CMOS double metal layer process technology to integrate 240,000 transistors on a 7.7×7.7 mm<sup>2</sup> die.}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Kusuda|first1=Masahiro|last2=Hirai|first2=Miho|last3=Suzuki|first3=Hiroaki|last4=Daito|first4=Masayuki|last5=Suzuki|first5=Chika|last6=Kimura|first6=Akiko|last7=Demura|first7=Shigeki|last8=Ishibashi|first8=Takashi|last9=Sato|first9=Syoichiro|title=低消費電力・低電圧動作のオリジナル32ビットRISCマイクロプロセッサV810|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=September 1992|volume=45|issue=8|pages=66–73|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/3259751?itemId=info%3Andljp%2Fpid%2F3259751&__lang=en|trans-title=V810-Low Power Consumption and Low Voltage Operation 32-bit RISC Microprocessor.|publisher=NEC Corporation|language=ja|format=image/jp2|issn=0285-4139|id=000000018731}}
</ref>

According to Renesas's documentation, the [[power consumption]] of the V850ES/Jx3-L implementation is about 70% of ARM Cortex-M3.<ref name="V850E2S-ovb"/>{{rp|14,15}}

The V810 was one of the most low-power 32-bit microcontroller products of the early 1990s. It operates at from 2.2&nbsp;V to 5.5&nbsp;V with a 5&nbsp;V 0.8&nbsp;μm (CZ4) [[fabrication process]].<ref name="logic process">
{{cite web |last1=Kuwata |first1=Takaaki |title=ロジックプロセス シリコンロジックプロセス ロジックプロセスの開発ものがたり |trans-title=Development story of silicon logic process |url=http://www.shmj.or.jp/dev_story/pdf/nec/nec_e07.pdf |publisher=Semiconductor History Museum of Japan |language=ja |access-date=23 September 2022}}
</ref>
Measured with Dhrystone MIPS, power dissipation is 500&nbsp;mW at 15MIPS and 40&nbsp;mW at 6&nbsp;MIPS, at 5&nbsp;V and 2.2&nbsp;V, respectively.  This specification can be achieved both by well considered instruction-set architecture and by precisely tuned 5-stage 1-clock pitch pipeline microarchitecture, both of which are the benefit of a simplified RISC architecture.

This ultra-low-power architecture was succeeded by V850/Sxn product line, which are still being mass-produced after 20 years. Most of the improved chips are produced using a 3.3&nbsp;V, 0.35μm (UC1) fabrication process, where the CPU core is precisely tuned to operate from 1.8&nbsp;V to 3.6&nbsp;V, working at 32.768&nbsp;kHz (sub-oscillator) to 16.78&nbsp;MHz (main-oscillator) with internal oscillator amplifier plus external resonator (crystal or ceramic).<ref name="SA1-PRESS"/>
Its power dissipation is 2.7&nbsp;mW/MIPS at 3.3&nbsp;V when made with a 0.35&nbsp;μm (UC1) [[fabrication process]], and 3.6&nbsp;mW/MIPS at 5&nbsp;V with a 0.35&nbsp;μm (CZ6) fabrication process. "Software STOP" stand-by mode for the mask ROM version of V850/SA1, whose internal watch timer operates at 3.3&nbsp;V with 32.768&nbsp;kHz sub-oscillator (I<sub>DD6</sub>), consumes typically only 8 μA electrical current. Subclock normal operation mode at 3.3&nbsp;V with 32.768&nbsp;kHz consumes 40 μA typically, 140 μA at the maximum. (I<sub>DD5</sub>)<ref>

{{cite book|title=V850/SA1 32-Bit Single-chip Microcontroller Hardware|date=August 2005|publisher=Renesas|edition=4.01|url=https://www.renesas.com/en/document/mah/v850sa1-hardware|ref=U12768EJ4V1UD00|language=en}}
</ref>{{rp|440, IDD5}}<ref name="V850/SA1"/>
Its 1.8&nbsp;V typical CPU operating current at 32.768&nbsp;kHz might be 22 [[μA]] (40&nbsp;μA ÷ 3.3&nbsp;V × 1.8&nbsp;V), where power dissipation should be 40&nbsp;[[μW]]. It corresponds to 1.0&nbsp;mW/MIPS (40&nbsp;μW ÷ 0.032768&nbsp;MHz ÷ 1.15&nbsp;DMIPS/MHz ÷ 1000).
<br/>
The V850/Sxn product line is also tuned for low noise, with both [[Electromagnetic interference|EMI]] and with [[Electromagnetic spectrum|EMS]]. The V850/SB1 and SB2 are especially tuned for low EMI noise with a 5&nbsp;V internal voltage regulator, which facilitates high sensitivity in receiving [[Radio frequency|RF]] for car radios.<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=OCHI|first1=MASATOSHI|last2=ISHIKAWA|first2=HIROTAKA|last3=TSUJI|first3=NOBUHIRO|last4=TAKEDA|first4=MITSURU|last5=SUTO|first5=SHIN'ICHI|last6=ISHIKAWA|first6=TATSUYA|title=32ビットRISCマイクロコントローラV850/SBXのEMIノイズ低減|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=2001-03-23|volume=54|issue=3|pages=41–44|url=http://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/public/20090422/200902108289418323|trans-title=EMI Noise Reduction of 32bit RISC Microcontroller V850/SBX.|publisher=NEC|language=ja|issn=0285-4139}}
</ref>{{rp|41–44}}

In 2011, NEC launched the 3rd generation microarchitecture V850ES ultra-low-power series, which achieves 1.43&nbsp;mW/MIPS at an operating voltage range of from 2.2&nbsp;V to 2.7&nbsp;V,<ref name="NEC: Press Release"/>
but this first implementation of V850ES microarchitecture seems to be incomplete compared with later generations of the same architecture.
Its "Sub-IDLE" stand-by mode for the mask ROM version of V850ES/SA2 and V850ES/SA3, whose internal RTC operate at 2.5&nbsp;V with 32.768&nbsp;kHz sub-oscillator (I<sub>DD6</sub>), consume typically only 5 μA electrical current. But, Subclock normal operation mode at 2.5&nbsp;V with 32.768&nbsp;kHz consumes typically 40 μA, 100 μA at the maximum.<ref>
{{cite book|title=V850ES/SA2, V850ES/SA3 32-Bit Single-Chip Microcontrollers Hardware|date=August 2005|publisher=Reneas|edition=2.01|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/023/U15905EJ2V1UD00.pdf|ref=U15905EJ2V1UD00|language=en}}{{dead link|fix-attempted=yes|date=May 2025}}
</ref>{{rp|509}}
Its 2.2&nbsp;V typical CPU operation current at 32.768&nbsp;kHz might be 31 μA (40&nbsp;μA ÷ 2.5&nbsp;V × 2.2&nbsp;V), where power dissipation should be 68 μW. This is about 1.7 times that of V850/SA1. It corresponds to 1.6&nbsp;mW/MIPS (68&nbsp;μW ÷ 0.032768&nbsp;MHz ÷ 1.3 DMIPS/MHz ÷ 1000).

The V850ES/JG3-L product line has ultra-low-power variants, the μPD70F3792, 793, and the μPD70F3841, 842. They can operate from 2.0&nbsp;V to 3.6&nbsp;V with typical electrical current of 18 μA at 32.768&nbsp;kHz,<ref name="JG3-L-UM">
{{cite book|title=V850ES/JG3-L User's manual: Hardware|date=2014-03-14|publisher=Renesas|edition=9.00|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/products/mpumcu/doc/v850/r01uh0165ej0900_v850esjg3l.pdf|language=en}}{{dead link|fix-attempted=yes|date=May 2025}}
</ref>{{rp|1002, 1041}} which should be 22 μW at 2.0&nbsp;V (18&nbsp;μA × 2.0&nbsp;V ÷ 3.3&nbsp;V × 2.0 V). This corresponds to 0.52&nbsp;mW/MIPS (22&nbsp;μW ÷ 0.032768&nbsp;MHz ÷ 1.3 DMIPS/MHz ÷ 1000). In addition, their sub-clock idle mode power consumption, with watch timer, should be typically 3.4 μW at 1.8&nbsp;V (3.5&nbsp;μA ÷ 3.3 V × 1.8&nbsp;V × 1.8&nbsp;V).<ref name="JG3-L-UM"/>{{rp|1002, 1041}}

The power consumption of the NA85E2 (V850E2) core is much larger compared with the NU85E (V850E1) core using the same CB-12L (UX4L)<ref name="logic process"/><ref name="UX4"/>
fabrication process. 
The reason is that the V850E2x core has a 128-bit [[instruction prefetch]] bus and more than one [[Instruction pipelining|instruction prefetch queue]],<ref>
{{cite web|title=RH850 & RL78 – Next Generation of Automotive Microcontrollers –|url=http://slideplayer.com/slide/7436709/|website=slideplayer.com}}
</ref>{{rp|16}}
while the average instruction length of the V800 series is 16 bits.<ref name="V810-seminar"/>{{rp|17}}
It means 16 instructions can be fetched from the memory at once, and the memory and prefetch circuits sleep fors 3 to 7 cycles for dual-pipeline [[superscalar architecture]]. 
This gap enlarges electrical current amplitude differences.
In addition, the peak [[electric current]] exceeds allowances for the [[voltage stabilizer]]s of mobile [[gadget]]s.
As for V850E2M CPU core, it is publicly introduced as 1.5&nbsp;mW/MIPS, 3 times that of former generations, although it should be able to take advantage of new [[Semiconductor device fabrication|fabrication process technologies]].<ref name="Biz-wire-2009"/>
Some mobile equipment avoids using dual-instruction execution (dual-pipeline [[superscalar]]), adopting the single-instruction (single-pipeline) execution setting to reduce electrical current amplitude differences.

===Instruction opcode table===
Each [[opcode|opcode (operation code)]] table is from ''User's Manual: Architecture'' (refer to [[#External links|external links.]]).

==== V810 (obsoleted) ====

*1st map opcodes

: All opcodes (operation codes) of the [[hardwired control unit|hardwired control]] operation are contained within the first 16-bit [[Word (computer architecture)|half-word]] of an instruction, from the [[most significant bit]] (MSB). A 64-word depth [[Read-only memory|ROM]] structure with [[Branch (computer science)|branch]] condition code table is enough for [[Central processing unit#Decode|decoding hardware]]. If a 16-bit literal [[operand]] is required, it is located in the second half-word. Microprogram control operations, bit strings, and floating-point arithmetic instructions are also located in the second 16-bit half-word. As a result, all the instructions have 16-bit and 32-bit 2-way form length. Unsigned load from [[memory mapped I/O]] is implemented as the <code>In</code> instruction. [[Arithmetic]] and [[Logical connective|logical]] instructions are not fully, but relatively, [[Orthogonal instruction set#RISC|orthogonal]].
: The V810 does not have saturation arithmetic instructions, but 1 additional instruction in format II, such as <code>SAT</code> which checks flags (<code>Overflow</code>, <code>Sign</code>, <code>Zero</code>, and <code>Half-word</code>) and rewrites the specified register, might be enough both for signed and unsigned, and for word and half-word, arithmetic operations.

{{cite journal|last1=Suzuki|first1=Hiroaki|last2=Sakai|first2=Toshichika|last3=Harigai|first3=Hisao|last4=Yano|first4=Yoichi|title=A 0.9-V, 2.5&nbsp;MHz CMOS 32-bit Microprocessor|journal=IEICE Transactions on Electronics|date=1995-04-25|volume=E78-C|issue=4|pages=389–393|url-access=subscription|url=http://search.ieice.org/bin/summary.php?id=e78-c_4_389&category=C&year=1995&lang=E|access-date=2018-01-09|issn=0916-8516|quote=<br/>Summary:<br/>A 32-bit RISC microprocessor "V810" that has 5-stage pipeline structure and a 1 Kbyte, direct-mapped instruction cache realizes 2.5&nbsp;MHz operation at 0.9 V with 2.0 mW power consumption. The supply voltage can be reduced to 0.75 V. To overcome narrow noise margin, all the signals are set to have rail-to-rail swing by pseudo-static circuit technique. The chip is fabricated by a 0.8 μm double metal-layer CMOS process technology to integrate 240,000 transistors on a 7.4 × 7.1 mm die.}}
</ref><ref name="Newer-gccVB">
{{cite web|title=A newer GCC compiler. « Virtual Boy Development Board « Forum « Planet Virtual Boy|url=http://www.planetvb.com/modules/newbb/viewtopic.php?topic_id=6456|website=www.planetvb.com|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127004426/http://www.planetvb.com/modules/newbb/viewtopic.php?topic_id=6456|archive-date=2018-01-27|url-status=dead}}
</ref><ref name="v851-broucher">

==SoC solutions==

===SoC IP cores===

In 1998, NEC started to provide the V850 family as an [[Application-specific integrated circuit|ASIC]] core, to expand its ASIC business.<ref name="CB-9-DM">
{{cite book|title=Design Manual: CB-9 Family VX/VM Type Core Library|publisher=NEC|edition=5th|url=http://pdf.datasheetcatalog.com/datasheet2/a/0ad1z0g461a8l8281h78s1px60wy.pdf|ref=A13195EJ5V1DM00|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211071716/http://pdf.datasheetcatalog.com/datasheet2/a/0ad1z0g461a8l8281h78s1px60wy.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-11|url-status=dead}}
</ref>
In addition, both the V850E1 CPU core named Nx85E<ref name="NA85E">
{{cite journal|last1=Sugimoto|first1=Hideki|last2=Sakairi|first2=Tetsuya|last3=Matoba|first3=Shoichiro|last4=Akaike|first4=Yukihiki|last5=Matsuyama|first5=Hideki|title=32ビットRISC CPU V850E搭載コア「NA85E」|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=March 1998|volume=51|issue=3|pages=36–39|url=http://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/detail?JGLOBAL_ID=200902160896928650|series=Special Issue: Semiconductor Devices. Semiconductor Devices for Computers Systems. Microcomputers.|trans-title=32bit RISC CPU Core "NA85E".|language=ja|issn=0285-4139}}
</ref><ref name="NB85E">
{{cite journal|last1=Sugimoto|first1=Hideki|last2=Ikeuchi|first2=Tooru|title=32ビツトRISC CPU V850E搭載コア「NB85E」 32bit RISC CPU Core "NB85E".|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=2000-03-30|volume=53|issue=4|pages=159–162|url=http://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/public/20090422/200902106221942927|series=Special Issue: Semiconductor Devices; Basic Technology|trans-title=32bit RISC CPU Core "NB85E".|publisher=NEC|language=ja|issn=0285-4139|id=200902106221942927}}
</ref>
and the V850E2 CPU core named Nx85E2,<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Sugimoto|first1=Hideki|title=RISCプロセッサNx85E2 CPU.|journal=NEC Technical Journal|date=2001-03-23|volume=54|issue=3|pages=30–33|url=http://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/detail?JGLOBAL_ID=200902198845610165|trans-title=RISC Processor Nx85E2 CPU.|publisher=NEC|language=ja|issn=0285-4139}}
</ref>
are also used for expanding its ASIC products business.
<br/>
Various [[System on a chip|SoCs]] utilize this core. In 2003, for example, Dotcast, Inc. used the NU85E core for a [[set top box]] receiver of [[Datacasting#MovieBeam|digital datacasting]] based on the dNTSC (data in [[NTSC]] video method<ref>
{{cite web|title=dNTSC|url=https://acronyms.thefreedictionary.com/dNTSC|website=The Free Dictionary}}
</ref>). This core is fabricated with CB-10 0.25μm 5-layered-metal process technology.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Simovich |first1=Slobodan| last2=Radivojevic |first2=Ivan P. |last3=Endres |first3=T. J. |last4=Bentson |first4=Tom |last5=Bingham |first5=Ray |last6=Blair |first6=Tony |last7=Cowling |first7=Tom |last8=Eylander |first8=Mark |last9=Fagan |first9=Rory |last10=Long |first10=Chris |last11=Longino |first11=Jim |last12=Olson |first12=Dan |last13=Subia |first13=Rollen |last14=Whitcomb |first14=Doug |title=ReX: A dNTSC Receiver System-on-Chip |conference=HotChips15 |date=2003 |pages=9–10 |url=http://www.hotchips.org/wp-content/uploads/hc_archives/hc15/2_Mon/8.dotcast.pdf |publisher=HotChips |language=en |archive-date=2016-04-23 |access-date=2018-02-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160423021353/http://www.hotchips.org/wp-content/uploads/hc_archives/hc15/2_Mon/8.dotcast.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref>{{rp|9–10}}

The NA85E2C core, which is developed using a 1.5&nbsp;V 150&nbsp;nm CB-12L (UX4L) fabrication process,<ref name="logic process"/><ref name="UX4">
{{cite press release|title=NEC Announces New Process Technology for World's Most Advanced System LSIs - World's First 0.13-micron Process Technology -|url=http://www.nec.co.jp/press/en/9910/0401.html|website=www.nec.co.jp|date=1999-10-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030205122033/http://www.nec.co.jp/press/en/9910/0401.html|archive-date=2003-02-05|url-status=dead}}
</ref>
has many [[errata]] (4 pages appendix in preliminary architecture manual,<ref>
{{cite book|author1=NEC Electronics|title=V850E2 32-bit Microprocessor Core Architecture|date=July 2004|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/024/U17135EJ1V1UM00.pdf|pages=230–233|edition=Preliminary|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127202707/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/024/U17135EJ1V1UM00.pdf|archive-date=2018-01-27|url-status=dead}}

plus a further, 7-page restrictions document<ref>
{{cite web|title=32-Bit Microcontrollers V850/ME3 Usage Restrictions|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/027/ZBG-CC-06-0039-E.pdf|language=en|date=2006-11-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180203064051/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/027/ZBG-CC-06-0039-E.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-03|url-status=dead}}
</ref>),
but which doesn't seem to matter, because this is a product with a long lifespan.

===FPGA prototyping systems for SoC===

[[FPGA prototyping]] systems for V850E1, V850E2, and V850E2M core-based SoCs were intensively developed to expand the SoC business. They comprised a V850 CPU core LSI (TEG, or Test Element Group) board and FPGA add-ons. Most SoC products were for mobile equipments, because the [[power dissipation]] of original V800-Series RISC architecture was much lower compared with [[Complex instruction set computer|CISC]].<ref name="1992-ARC-06"/><ref name="V850E2S-ovb"/><ref name="IEIEC-1995"/> 
It is similar to the [[ARM architecture family|ARM architecture]] that is widely used for mobile gadgets.

==Strategic confusion==

Around 2011–2014, Renesas Electronics extensively expanded the V850E2 product line,<ref>
{{cite press release|title=Renesas Electronics Introduces 4th-Generation V850 Microcontrollers Series with 74 Individual Devices for Automotive Body, Dashboard, Chassis and Safety Applications|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/about/press-center/news/2010/news20101104.html|publisher=Renesas|date=2010-11-04}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=Renesas - New MCUs for automotive body, dashboard, chassis and safety applications|url=https://www.electropages.com/2010/11/renesas-new-mcus-for-automotive-body-dashboard-chassis-and-safety-applications/|website=www.electropages.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130726162650/https://www.electropages.com/2010/11/renesas-new-mcus-for-automotive-body-dashboard-chassis-and-safety-applications/|archive-date=2013-07-26|url-status=dead}}
</ref>
but this high-paced expansion brought much confusion. For example, as of 2018, some have requested that V850E2/xxn products be replaced with RH850/xnx ones.<ref>
{{cite web|title=V850ES/Fx3|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/products/microcontrollers-microprocessors/v850/v850esfx/v850esfx3.html|website=Renesas Electronics|access-date=2018-01-28}}
</ref>

In addition, in 2012 Renesas started to intensively promote the migration from ten-year-old V850ES/Jx3 product lines to the newly produced V850E2/Jx4, such as for Ethernet and USB applications,<ref>
{{cite web|title= V850E2/Jx4 Series Ultra Low Power 32 bit MCUs – Migration from V850ES/Jx3 MCUs –
|url=https://elearning.renesas.com/pluginfile.php/355/mod_folder/content/0/V850_Family/V850_Jx3_to_Jx4_Migration.pdf?forcedownload=1|website=Renesas}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=V850/Jx4 Series Ultra Low Power 32 bit MCUs|url=https://elearning.renesas.com/pluginfile.php/355/mod_folder/content/0/V850_Family/V850_Jx4_Overview.pdf?forcedownload=1|website=Renesas|date=March 2012}}
</ref>
but the newer products are not listed on their website, as of 2018.<ref name="renesas_v850"/>

Currently,{{As of?|date=November 2021}} Renesas Electronics is designing a "dual" "lockstep" system, but its predecessor NEC V60-V80 had "multiple modular" lockstep mechanism called FRM,<ref name="compcon1988">{{Cite book | doi = 10.1109/CMPCON.1988.4824 | chapter = V60/V70 microprocessor and its systems support functions | title = Digest of Papers. COMPCON Spring 88 Thirty-Third IEEE Computer Society International Conference | pages = [https://archive.org/details/compconspring8830000ieee/page/36 36–42] | year = 1988 | last1 = Yano | first1 = Y. | last2 = Koumoto | first2 = Y. | last3 = Sato | first3 = Y. | isbn = 0-8186-0828-5 | s2cid = 9186701 | chapter-url = https://archive.org/details/compconspring8830000ieee/page/36 }}</ref>
either with roll-back by "retry" or with roll-forward by "exception" for each fault detected instruction.

In addition, the NEC V60-V80 has several implementations of [[UNIX System V]] port product releases, one of which is "real-time UNIX RX/UX-832"<ref name="RX-UX-832">
{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0165-6074(89)90105-1| title = Real-time UNIX operating system: RX-UX 832| journal = Microprocessing and Microprogramming| volume = 27| issue = 1–5| pages = 533–538| date = August 1989| last1 = Mizuhashi | first1 = Yukiko | last2 = Teramoto | first2 = Msanoro |quote= <br/>Abstract:<br/>This paper describes requirements for real-time UNIX operating systems, design concept and the implementation of RX-UX 832 real-time UNIX operating system for v60/v70 microprocessor which are NEC's 32-bit microprocessors. RX-UX 832 is implemented adopting the building block structure, composed of three modules, real-time kernel, file-server and Unix supervisor. To guarantee a real-time responsibility, several enhancements were introduced such as, fixed priority task scheduling scheme, contiguous block file system and fault tolerant functions.<br/>Thus, RX-UX 832 allows system designers to use standard Unix as its man-machine interface to build fault tolerant systems with sophisticated operability and provides high-quality software applications on the high performance microchips. }}
</ref>
(here, 832 stands for the μPD70832 (V80), not V832). Its multiprocessor implementation is called MUSTARD (Multiprocessor Unix for Embedded Real-Time Systems), which can operate a maximum of 8 processors simultaneously, and its lockstep mechanism was dynamically configurable.<ref name="Suzuki1992">
{{cite book|author=Norihisa Suzuki|title=Shared Memory Multiprocessing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hyn9Cqf8PZsC&pg=PA195|date=January 1992|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-19322-1|page=195}}
</ref>

In 2001, both [[NEC Corporation]] and [[Synopsys, Inc.]], announced they had agreed to promote the V850E as DesignWare IP core.<ref name="DesignWare-NEC"/><ref name="DesignWare-Synopsys"/>
But as of 2018, the V850E is not listed on DesignWare libraries.<ref>
{{cite web|title=Synopsys DesignWare Library of Design and Verification IP|url=https://www.synopsys.com/designware-ip/soc-infrastructure-ip/designware-library.html|website=www.synopsys.com|access-date=2018-01-29}}
</ref>

[[Lucent Technologies]] and [[Texas Instruments]] once licensed the V850 and V850E SoC cores, respectively,<ref>
{{cite web|title=Lucent Technologies Licenses NEC's 32-Bit V850 Family Microcontroller Core {{!}} EE Times|url=https://www.eetimes.com/lucent-technologies-licenses-necs-32-bit-v850-family-microcontroller-core/|website=EE Times|date=1997-12-16}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=Corporate Liaisons: Intel & Sun Announce Alliance. NEC and Lucent Sign Agrmt. Seagate & Compaq Ink Dvpt Agrmt.|url=https://www.hpcwire.com/1997/12/19/corporate-liaisons-intel-sun-announce-alliance-nec-lucent-sign-agrmt-seagate-compaq-ink-dvpt-agrmt/|website=HPCwire|date=19 December 1997}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite press release|title=Texas Instruments Expands DSP-Based SLI TImeBuilderTM Portfolio With License of NEC's V850E Embedded Processor Architecture|url=http://www.nec.co.jp/press/en/9903/2901.html|publisher=NEC|date=1999-03-29}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=組み込みニュース|url=http://www.kumikomi.net/i/news/2001/10/01_03.html|website=www.kumikomi.net|language=ja|trans-title=Embedded News|date=2001-10-01}}
</ref>
but those devices cannot be found.

In 2006, [[Metrowerks]] developed the [[CodeWarrior]] compiler for the V850, which was one of the main compilers for the V850,<ref name="devtools-2006"/>
but around 2010, they discontinued support.

Also in 2006, NEC did not give any roadmap for the V850 family as SoC cores.<ref name="NEC-Tech-J-2006"/> The V850E2 core, developed in 2004, was described as the last, best core for SoC applications. However, NEC introduced ARM9 (arm v5) and ARM11 (arm v6), especially for mobile equipment.
This decision suddenly decreased the net profit of LSI devices, because of the royalty for using ARM, and thus price competition with other ARM SoC providers. The sales revenue of "V850 total solutions", such as development tools, real-time OS, middle-ware packages, and in-circuit emulators, also decreased. The number of V850 devices sold also suddenly decreased, because mobile equipment manufacturer were the major customers of V850E1 and V850E2 cores at that moment.<ref>
{{cite press release|title=NEC Electronics and Renesas to Integrate Business Operations Establishment of the World's Third Largest Semiconductor Company|url=http://www.nec.co.jp/press/en/0904/2703.html|publisher=NEC Corporation|date=April 27, 2009}}
</ref>

In 2008, KMC (Kyoto Mictocomputer), which is one of the major and of the first providers of in-circuit emulators for the V850 family, announced "exeGCC" being updated from Rel. 3 to Rel. 4,<ref>
{{cite web|title=組み込みCPU対応コンパイラexeGCCの新バージョンを発表|url=https://www.kmckk.co.jp/news3/r081111_3.html|website=www.kmckk.co.jp|publisher=Kyoto Microcomputer|language=ja|date=2008-11-12}}
</ref>
but it excluded the V850 from this updating list, which added PowerPC and ARM v7. KMC chose SH-4A and ARM v7, instead of V850 and RH850,<ref>
{{cite web|title=組み込み用GNU Cコンパイラ exeGCC|trans-title=exeGCC: GNU C compilere for emmbedded targetes|url=https://www.kmckk.co.jp/gcc4/index.html|website=www.kmckk.co.jp|language=ja}}
</ref>
though it had been working closely with NEC and Renesas Electronics.<ref name="devtools-2006"/>

The V850 CPU cores run [[uClinux]],<ref name="uClinux">{{cite web|author=D. Jeff Dionne |author2=Michael Durrant |title=Embedded Linux/Microcontroller Project |url=http://www.uclinux.org/ports/|website=uClinux |access-date=2018-01-26|archive-date=2017-02-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170212000213/http://www.uclinux.org/ports/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
but on October 9, 2008, [[Linux kernel]] support for the V850 was removed in revision 2.6.27.,<ref name="Linux_2_6_27">
{{cite web|title=Linux_2_6_27 - Linux Kernel Newbies|url=https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_2_6_27#head-b14ab696e23019ae4b6362c5816bcd23a55240ce|website=kernelnewbies.org}}
</ref> because NEC stopped its maintenance.<ref>
{{cite web|last1=Bunk|first1=Adrian|last2=Torvalds|first2=Linus|title=remove the v850 port|url=https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=f606ddf42fd4edc558eeb48bfee66d2c591571d2|website=git.kernel.org|date=2008-07-24|quote=<br/>Trying to compile the v850 port brings many compile errors, one of them exists since at least kernel 2.6.19.<br/>There also seems to be no one willing to bring this port back into a usable state.<br/>This patch therefore removes the v850 port.<br/> If anyone ever decides to revive the v850 port the code will still be available from older kernels, and it wouldn't be impossible for the port to reenter the kernel if it would become actively maintained again.}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=Search Results for: lsi.nec.co.jp|url=https://www.systutorials.com/linux-kernel-changelogs/?s=lsi.nec.co.jp|website=Linux Kernel Changelogs|date=2018-02-06}}{{dead link|fix-attempted=yes|date=May 2025}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web|title=uCLinux|url=http://www.ic.nec.co.jp/micro/uclinux/eng/|website=www.ic.nec.co.jp/micro/uclinux/|quote=<br/>Link missing for <www.ic.nec.co.jp/micro/uclinux/>}}
</ref>
The person in charge of V850 Linux kernel maintenance was moved from NEC to Renesas by its merger, but his new job was compiler design and never returned to Linux kernel maintenance.<ref>
{{cite web |title=(24) Miles Bader {{!}} LinkedIn |url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/miles-bader-22822610}}
</ref>
This corporate decision prevented the possibility of porting to [[Android (operating system)|Android]].<ref name="android-kernel">
{{cite web|title=Kernel {{!}} Android Open Source Project|url=https://source.android.com/devices/architecture/kernel/|website=Android Open Source Project}}</ref>
As of 2018, Renesas Electronics mainly focuses Linux kernel support on [[SuperH|SH3/SH4]] and [[M32R]] processors.

===Operating systems===

V850 [[Operating system]]s are mostly [[Real-time operating system|real-time]].

Some operating systems require a [[memory protection unit]] (MPU) to divide [[Task (computing)|task]]s (or [[Thread (computing)|thread]]s) strictly for [[Reliability (computer networking)|reliability]] and safety reasons. In such cases, the v850e2v3 (Gen. 3) [[microarchitecture]], or above, is required.

====ITRON based real-time OS====

''[[ITRON]]'' is an [[open standard]] specification of [[real-time OS]] (RTOS), which is major in Japan.
Its specification is defined under the leadership of [[Ken Sakamura]], as a part of [[TRON project]], the initialr I standing for "Industrial". Because the ITRON specification defines interface and skeleton only, each vendor has its own implementation.

====AUTOSAR, OSEK/VDX compliant real-time OS====

''[[AUTOSAR]]'' is an [[open systems architecture]] of [[operating system]] for the [[automotive industry]]. Its purpose is to standardize [[electronic control unit]]s (ECU) for [[automotive engine]]s. [[AUTOSAR]] is an upward compatible specification of [[OSEK/VDX]], which is also a German [[consortium]] established in 1993.

In Japan, this research was started in 2006, as a joint project by [[JAIST]] and [[DENSO]]. Renesas Electronics joined this project in 2009.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Aoki|first1=Toshiaki|editor1-last=Nakajima|editor1-first=Shin|editor2-last=Talpin|editor2-first=Jean-Pierre|editor3-last=Toyoshima|editor3-first=Masumi|editor4-last=Yu|editor4-first=Huafeng|title=Practical Application of Formal Methods to Automotive Systems|journal=NII Shonan Meeting Report|date=2016-03-21|volume=2016|issue=5|page=16|url=http://shonan.nii.ac.jp/shonan/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/No.2016-5.pdf|series=Architecture-Centric Modeling, Analysis, and Verification of Cyber-Physical Systems|issn=2186-7437|archive-date=2018-02-25|access-date=2018-02-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180225210113/http://shonan.nii.ac.jp/shonan/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/No.2016-5.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
Because the current RH850 and V850 processors are principally targeted at the automotive industry, it is a strategical product of Renesas Electronics. However, its documentation is only available in Japanese, as its main customer is [[Toyota Motor Corporation]].

*Renesas: ''RV850'' (documents are in Japanese only)<ref>

==Hardware development tools==

===ICE (In-circuit emulators)===

Most [[in-circuit emulator]]s, such as Renesas's ''IE850'' (formerly ''IECUBE2''),<ref name="IE850"/>
can be used for both the V850 family and the RH850 family, but may require [[firmware]] updating.
The latest "trace function" of the [[JTAG]] (''N-Wire''<ref>
{{cite web|title=PCMCIA N-Wire Card IE-V850E1-CD-NW|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/023/U16975EE2V0PL00.pdf|website=Renesas Electronics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180129004336/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/023/U16975EE2V0PL00.pdf|archive-date=2018-01-29|url-status=dead}}
</ref>) based in-circuit emulator is upgraded from the ''N-Trace'' ([[single-ended signaling]])<ref name="usbid_dti53np2">
{{cite journal|last1=Matsumoto|first1=Toshinobu|title=NEW EMULATION METHODOLOGY SUPPORTING HIGH-SPEED MICROCOMPUTERS|journal=NEC Device Technology International|volume=1999|issue=53|url=https://www.usbid.com/datasheets/usbid/2000/2000-q2/dti53np2.pdf|publisher=NEC|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180209123748/https://www.usbid.com/datasheets/usbid/2000/2000-q2/dti53np2.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-09|url-status=dead}}
</ref>
to the ''[[Aurora (protocol)|Aurora]] Trace'' ([[differential signaling]]).<ref>
{{cite web|title=Trace32 development tools support Renesas automotive MCU: Lauterbach|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/about/web-magazine/edge/partner/15-lauterbach.html|website=Renesas Electronics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180129004424/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/about/web-magazine/edge/partner/15-lauterbach.html|archive-date=2018-01-29|url-status=dead}}
</ref>

====JTAG N-Wire and N-Trace type====

N-Wire and N-Trace<ref>
{{cite web|title=IDT JTAG/EJTAG Devices|url=http://datasheet.datasheetarchive.com/originals/library/Datasheets-UD1/DSAUD001730.pdf|publisher=Integrated Device Technology, Inc.|date=2000|quote=<br/>The vast majority of the competition's offerings have included a JTAG Test Access Port (TAP). Recently, products have been arriving with more enhanced capabilities, such as N-Wire/N-Trace from NEC, RISCWatch from IBM, and COP from Motorola. These versions of Enhanced JTAG perform relatively the same functions and use the traditional JTAG TAP with a couple additional pins for greater control.}}
</ref><ref name="usbid_dti53np2"/><ref>
{{cite web|title=64-bit RISC MPU uses superscalar scheme {{!}} EE Times|url=https://www.eetimes.com/64-bit-risc-mpu-uses-superscalar-scheme/|website=EE Times|date=2001-07-30}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite book|title=Data sheet: VR5500 64-/32-BIT MICROPROCESSOR|date=September 2002|publisher=NEC|page=5|edition=2nd|url=http://pdf.eepw.com.cn/u20091120/c17091efbd680e59cd903a2974e48f02.pdf|ref=U15700EJ1V0DS01|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230608010617/http://pdf.eepw.com.cn/u20091120/c17091efbd680e59cd903a2974e48f02.pdf|archive-date=2023-06-08|url-status=dead}}
</ref>
is a [[JTAG]]-based debugging interface specification, which circuit implementation is called TAP Controller (Test Access Port controller),<ref>
{{cite web|title=Training JTAG Interface|url=http://www2.lauterbach.com/pdf/training_jtag.pdf|website=lauterbach.com|publisher=Lauterbach|pages=13–15|language=en}}
</ref>
primarily compiled by [[Philips N.V.]] (currently [[NXP Semiconductors]]). But it is perhaps not disclosed publicly in its earlier stage. As the result, each semiconductor and [[in-circuit emulator]] vendor implemented similar interfaces independently. Nowadays, it is standardized by ''IEEE 1149.1 Working Group''.<ref>
{{cite web|title=JTAG IEEE 1149.1 Standard WG|url=https://grouper.ieee.org/groups/1149/1/|website=[[IEEE]]}}
</ref>

====Nexus and Aurora trace type====

''[[Nexus (standard)|Nexus]]'' or ''IEEE-ISTO 5001-2003'' is a standard [[debugging]] interface for [[embedded system]]s.
<br/>
''[[Aurora (protocol)|Aurora]]'' is a high speed signal transfer specification. Its [[data link layer]] [[communications protocol]] is a point-to-point [[serial communications|serial links]], and [[physical layer]] is a high speed [[differential signaling]].

*[[Lauterbach (company)|Lauterbach]]: Trace32: PowerTrace for NEXUS<ref>
{{cite book|title=PowerTrace for NEXUS|date=2013-06-14|publisher=Lauterbach|url=http://www.lauterbach.com/doc/nexus.pdf|language=en}}
</ref>
*{{Proper name|iSystem}}: BlueBox iC5000 and iC5700 (Nexus), iC6000 (Aurora)<ref name="Renesas RH850 Microcontrollers"/><ref>{{cite web|title=On-Chip Analyzer|url=http://tridentinfosol.com/onchip.html|website=Trident infosol|language=en|access-date=2020-08-20|archive-date=2019-07-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190716200618/http://tridentinfosol.com/onchip.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Flash ROM programmers===

Because the V850 family is developed as a [[single chip microcontroller]], every product integrates [[non-volatile memory]]. In its first stage, it was [[one-time programmable]] or [[UV EPROM]] type, but in V853, V850/xxn Series, and later, it becomes [[flash memory]] type.

====Gang writers (gang programmers)====

A ''gang writer'', or a ''gang programmer'', is an old [[terminology]] for [[programmable ROM]] [[Programmer (hardware)|writers, or programmers]]. Its name comes from that it steals the binary code from one device, and write it to several others simultaneously. This ''read device'' is sometimes called a ''master device''. For mass production use, a dedicated attachment board with "a set of sockets", i.e. "a gang", is needed. As usual, instead of a programmed master device, an [[object code]] file can be copied from a PC via download cable, or from a USB stick. Most ''gang writers'' accept [[ASCII]]-format files such as ''[[Intel HEX]]'' and [[SREC (file format)|Motorola ''SREC'']], or binary format files such as ''[[Executable and Linkable Format|ELF]]''.

This method is suitable for mass production.

*TESSERA Technology Inc.: ''Stick GANG Writer''<ref>{{cite web|title=TESSERA TECHNOLOGY INC.|url=http://www.tessera.co.jp/eng/swriter.html|website=www.tessera.co.jp|language=ja|access-date=2018-02-25|archive-date=2017-11-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171119080831/http://www.tessera.co.jp/eng/swriter.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

====Programming service providers====

Flash ROM programming [[service provider]]s exist in most countries.

*Minato Holdings, Inc.

:[[:ja:ミナトホールディングス|Minato Holdings, Inc. (in Japanese)]]<ref>
{{cite web|title=ROM Programming Service|url=https://www.minato.co.jp/en/product/romw/|website=MINATO HOLDINGS INC.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180221002848/https://www.minato.co.jp/en/product/romw/|archive-date=2018-02-21|url-status=dead}}
</ref> is a Japanese company that started as an [[automated test equipment]] vendor for memory LSIs. Nowadays, it provides [[flash ROM]] programming services for various devices, including V850 and RH850, with its own ''gang writers'' and ''full automatic device handler'' machines.

====On board programming with ICE====

Most [[JTAG]]-based [[in-circuit emulator]]s have an ''on board'' flash ROM programming function via a debug port,
<br/>
which may be according to ''IEEE standard 1532-2002'', a standard for in-system configuration of programmable components.<ref>
{{cite web|title=What is the IEEE 1532 Standard? {{!}} Keysight (formerly Agilent's Electronic Measurement)|url=https://edadocs.software.keysight.com/kkbopen/what-is-the-ieee-1532-standard-589751407.html}}
</ref>

====Direct connection via RS-232C====

If the target board has a ''[[RS-232C]]'' connector and a transceiver (driver/receiver) IC, such as ''ICL32xx'',<ref>
{{cite book|title=ICL3221, ICL3222, ICL3223, ICL3232, ICL3241, ICL3243: Data sheet|date=2015-09-01|edition=22.00|url=https://www.intersil.com/content/dam/Intersil/documents/icl3/icl3221-22-23-32-41-43.pdf}}
</ref>
for the ''UARTx'' peripheral function of V850 device, flash ROM programming with a directly connected [[Personal computer|PC]] might be available (depends on devices<ref name="Programmer-Support">
{{cite web|title=List of MCUs supported by Renesas Flash Programmer V2|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/search/keyword-search.html#q=r20ut0676ej&genre=document|website=Renesas Electronics}}
</ref>{{rp|16–24}}
).
The ''Renesas Flash Programmer'' software ''V2''<ref>
{{cite web|title=Renesas Flash Programmer (Programming GUI) [V2]|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/products/software-tools/tools/programmer/renesas-flash-programmer-programming-gui-v2.html|website=Renesas Electronics}}
</ref>
or ''V3''<ref>
{{cite web|title=Renesas Flash Programmer (Programming GUI)|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/products/software-tools/tools/programmer/renesas-flash-programmer-programming-gui.html|website=Renesas Electronics}}
</ref>
is required.

====Dedicated on board programmer====

On-board programming is also available via ''UARTx'' or ''CSIx+HS'' peripherals on V850 devices by using dedicated programmer hardware (depends on devices<ref name="Programmer-Support"/>{{rp|16–24}}).

*Renesas: ''PG-FP6''<ref>
{{cite book|title=PG-FP6 V1.01 Flash Memory Programmer User's Manual|date=2018-02-20|publisher=Renesas|edition=1.00|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/products/tool/doc/012/r20ut4254ej0100-pgfp6.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180303050414/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/products/tool/doc/012/r20ut4254ej0100-pgfp6.pdf|archive-date=2018-03-03|url-status=dead}}

*Renesas ''PG-1500'' (obsoleted)
:Renesas ''PG-1500''<ref>
{{cite book|title=PG-1500 User's Manual|date=1997-05-01|publisher=Renesas|edition=4.00|url=https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/021/U11940EJ4V0UM00.pdf|ref=U11940EJ4V0UM00|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226211533/https://www.renesas.com/en-us/doc/DocumentServer/021/U11940EJ4V0UM00.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-26|url-status=dead}}
</ref> is a [[programmable ROM]] writer compatible with ''27C1001A''<ref>
{{cite book|title=UPD27C1001A Data Sheet|publisher=NEC|url=http://datasheet.datasheetarchive.com/originals/scans/Scans-063/DSA2IH00126439.pdf}}
</ref> devices, [[UV EPROM]], or [[Programmable read-only memory|one-time PROM]] (OTP). This writer reads a ''silicon signature''<ref>
{{cite web|last1=Jordan|first1=Larry T. |title=US 4,451,903A: Method and device for encoding product and programming information in semiconductors|url=http://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/.piw?PageNum=0&docid=04451903 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226211537/http://pdfpiw.uspto.gov/.piw?PageNum=0&docid=04451903 |archive-date=2018-02-26 |website=United States Patent and Trademark Office|language=en|format=PDF|date=1981-09-18}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite book|title=Certain EPROM, EEPROM, Flash Memory and Flash Microcontroller Semiconductor Devices and Products Containing Same, Inv. 337-TA-395|publisher=DIANE Publishing|isbn=978-1-4578-2497-5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MjJncNuhT2wC&q=silicon+signature+JEDEC&pg=PA56|language=en}}
</ref> from each device before programming, by asserting 12.5&nbsp;V to the ''A9'' (address #9) terminal. It must NOT be used for modern [[flash ROM]] burning.
